dataset.what_one_row_represents: One film, in one Oscar-eligibility year, with its IMDb 'connections' count and that year's annual_share among all referenced films.
dataset.geographic_scope: Global film catalogue, but heavily Western-biased (per IMDb crowdsourcing). Ceremony field follows the U.S. Academy Awards.

ana_01.label: Dataset shape and Best Picture coverage
ana_01.content: The dataset spans 29,046 rows covering 27,826 unique films with oscars_year 1928-2017. Among those, 89 are Best Picture winners (`result == 'W'`) and a further 449 are Best Picture nominees (`result == 'N'`). The remaining 28,508 rows are films that were never nominated for Best Picture but appear in IMDb's connection network for their release year. The total IMDb 'connections' tallied across the dataset is 388,165.

ana_02.label: The 16-year drought: no Best Picture winner has been the most-referenced film of its year since 2000
ana_02.content: From oscars_year 2001 through 2016 — 16 consecutive years — no Best Picture winner was the single most-referenced film of its year. The most recent winner to top its own year was Gladiator (2000, 304 references, 6.4% annual share). The longest drought before that was the early-1980s slump (Ordinary People, Chariots of Fire, Gandhi, Terms of Endearment, Amadeus, Out of Africa, Platoon, The Last Emperor, Rain Man — eight winners between 1980 and 1988 with no #1).

ana_03.label: Decade-by-decade collapse of the average winner's annual share
ana_03.content: Mean annual_share of Best Picture winners peaked in the 1970s at 9.4% — that decade saw The Godfather, Rocky, and Patton each reach #1 in their year, with The Godfather alone capturing 33.7% of all 1972 references. By the 2010s, mean annual_share has collapsed to 1.5% — a 6.4x drop. Median year-rank has roughly tripled, from 3.5 in the 1970s to 8.0 in the 2010s. The percentage of decade winners that hit #1 in their own year falls from 30% (1960s, 1970s) to zero in the 2010s.

calculation.output: 1970: mean_share=9.44%, median_rank=3.5, pct_top1=30%\n2010: mean_share=1.48%, median_rank=8.0, pct_top1=0%

ana_04.label: BP winners hit #1 in their year only 14 of 89 times — and only twice since 1991
ana_04.content: Of the 89 Best Picture winners in the dataset, only 14 (15.7%) were also the most-referenced film of their oscars_year. That set: All Quiet on the Western Front (1930), It Happened One Night (1934), Casablanca (1943), The Lost Weekend (1945), The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), West Side Story (1961), Lawrence of Arabia (1962), The Sound of Music (1965), Patton (1970), The Godfather (1972), Rocky (1976), The Silence of the Lambs (1991), Titanic (1997), and Gladiator (2000). The post-1990 hit rate is 3 in 27 (Silence of the Lambs, Titanic, Gladiator).

ana_05.label: Empire Strikes Back vs Ordinary People: the largest unnominated-film snub on record
ana_05.content: In 1980, the Best Picture winner Ordinary People accumulated 94 IMDb references; The Empire Strikes Back, which was not nominated for Best Picture, accumulated 1,748 — 18.6 times as many. That gap is the largest in the dataset between a Best Picture winner and an unnominated film from the same year. The 1977 Annie Hall vs Star Wars matchup is almost identical (274 vs 4,965, an 18.1x ratio).

ana_06.label: In 74 of 89 winning years, an unnominated film out-referenced the Best Picture winner
ana_06.content: In 74 out of 89 (83%) of the years that produced a Best Picture winner, at least one film that was never even nominated for Best Picture has accumulated more IMDb references than the actual winner. The 16 exceptions are years like 1942 (Casablanca) and 1972 (The Godfather), where the winner is also the year's anchor cultural text.

ana_07.label: The five worst-ranked Best Picture winners by year-rank
ana_07.content: Five Best Picture winners ranked 22nd or worse among the films of their own oscars_year: Cavalcade (1933, rank 37), The Last Emperor (1987, rank 36), Tom Jones (1963, rank 29), Spotlight (2015, rank 25), and The Life of Emile Zola (1937, rank 22). ana_08.label: Casablanca's 48.7% — the largest annual_share of any Best Picture winner ever
ana_08.content: Casablanca (oscars_year 1943) holds the record for the highest annual_share of any Best Picture winner: 48.7% — meaning Casablanca alone accounts for almost half of all IMDb-tracked references to films from its year. The runner-up that year, Lassie Come Home, has just 4.8% — Casablanca's 1,454 references dwarf the next-most-referenced 1943 film by an order of magnitude.

calculation.output: Casablanca 1454 0.487 W rank 1\nLassie Come Home 143 0.048 NaN rank 2

ana_09.label: The People's Best Pictures: a 16-year list dominated by blockbusters
ana_09.content: If we treat the year's most-referenced film as the 'people's pick', then since 2001 the list looks completely different from the Academy's. It includes The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), Spider-Man (2002), Saw (2004), Star Wars Episode III (2005), Transformers (2007), Twilight (2008), Avatar (2009), Inception (2010), Thor (2011), The Avengers (2012), Frozen (2013), Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), The Force Awakens (2015), and Batman v Superman (2016). Only three of these 16 'people's picks' were even nominated for Best Picture: Fellowship of the Ring, Avatar, and Inception. Eleven were never nominated at all.

ana_10.label: Star Wars 1977 commands 55% of its year's references — the highest single-year share in the dataset
ana_10.content: Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope holds the dataset record for raw references (4,965) and for highest annual_share by any film (55.2% of all 1977 references). It was nominated for Best Picture and lost to Annie Hall (274 references, 3.0% annual_share); the gap is 18.1x. The Wizard of Oz (1939) is second on the all-time list with 3,291 references and 50.3% annual_share — and lost Best Picture to Gone with the Wind, which itself has a respectable 1,154 references but came second in its own year.

ana_11.label: The 1980s collapse: BP winners fell from 9% of top-100 references to 2%
ana_11.content: Looking at the share of all top-100 references that go to films that won Best Picture in their decade: in the 1940s and 1970s this peaked near 9-10%; by the 1980s it crashed to 2.1%, and the 2010s sit at just 1.4% — a record low. This metric captures footprint: even when winners are not #1 in their year, are the winners as a group still capturing meaningful weight in the cultural memory of their decade? The answer for the post-1980 era is no.

ana_12.label: 2015: Spotlight (rank 25) vs The Force Awakens (rank 1) — the steepest mismatch of the 2010s
ana_12.content: In 2015, Best Picture went to Spotlight, which sits at rank 25 of its year with 31 references and 0.78% annual_share — the worst rank held by any 21st-century winner. The same year's most-referenced film, Star Wars: The Force Awakens, has 358 references (11.5x more) and 9.0% annual_share. This single year captures the entire thesis: an Academy-celebrated film that the broader culture barely cites, paired with a non-nominated blockbuster that the culture cannot stop referencing.

caveats.content: References data is a frozen end-of-2017 IMDb snapshot, so 2017 is partial and films released late in 2017 (e.g. The Shape of Water) are absent — that is why the analysis stops at oscars_year 2016 for narrative claims.

IMDb's connection network is heavily Western-biased — non-Anglophone films are systematically under-counted. The 'recency problem' (older films have had longer to accumulate references) is real but is partly neutralised by the within-year annual_share metric used here.

Crowdsourcing introduces enthusiasm bias: cult films and franchises generate more reference adds than equally influential 'serious' cinema. Some recent connection entries are low-signal (e.g., actors plugging films on chat shows).

The dataset retains a few films that were not technically Best Picture-eligible (Metropolis 1927, Steamboat Willie 1929, Un Chien Andalou 1929) for early-year orientation. Their year_rank values still appear in the data.
